:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The formula for the area of a general triangle is

$$
\mathcal{A}=\frac{1}{2}{\color{red}{a}}{\color{blue}{b}}\sin{C},
$$

where $\color{red}a$ and $\color{blue}b$ are two sides of the triangle and $C$ is the measure of the angle between those sides (called the **included angle**).

We'll prove this result at the end of the lesson.

To demonstrate how this works, suppose that we want to calculate the area of the non-right-angled triangle below:

![](images/4b/4b0fb75f9b2eaf3d0237d8cfe2e31bc27b02425b6cffa8d15f27d6de03f60838.png)

Let's call the lengths of the sides $BC = \color{red}{a}$ and $AC ={\color{blue}{b}}.$ For the triangle above we have
${\color{red}a=10},$ ${\color{blue}b=12},$ and  $m\angle C=45^{\circ}.$

Therefore, the area of our triangle is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 10\cdot 12\cdot \operatorname{sin}{45}^{∘} \\  & =60\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =30\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Find the area of $\triangle{ABC}$ below. Round your answer to two decimal places.

![](images/dc/dc625408598aa3cbfda44ec877c9a26ab563dee9fcf757192fcf2cf8411f606a.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The formula for the area of the triangle is 

$$
\mathcal{A}=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin{C},
$$

where $\angle{C}$ is between the sides of lengths $a$ and $b.$ 

Here, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =CB=58 \\ b & =CA=40 \\ m∠C & ={31}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since 

$$
\sin{31^{\circ}} = 0.515\,038
$$

rounded to six decimal places,  we calculate the area as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 58\cdot 40\operatorname{sin}⁡{31}^{∘} \\  & =1160\cdot (0.515\,038) \\  & ≈597.44,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating the Area of a Triangle

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
The area of ​​the triangle $\triangle ABC$ is $24\sqrt{2} \text{ cm}^2.$ Find $AB.$

![](images/e9/e93e732bd04cfda304c2098087548a638d8d869ccf8b1050235e8207825875d3.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The formula for the area of the triangle is 

$$
\mathcal{A}=\dfrac{1}{2}bc\sin{A},
$$

where $\angle{A}$ is between the sides of lengths $b$ and $c.$ 

Here

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =AB, \\ b & =AC=12\text{ cm}, \\ m∠A & ={45}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since 

$$
\sin{45^{\circ}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2},
$$

we can calculate $c=AB,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot c\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ 24\sqrt{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 12\cdot c\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{45}^{∘} \\ 24\sqrt{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 12\cdot c\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\ 24\cancel{\sqrt{2}} & =3\cancel{\sqrt{2}}c \\ 24 & =3c \\ c & =8\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $AB = 8\,\textrm{cm}.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating an Angle or Side of a Triangle Given the Area of a Triangle

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Rounded to the nearest integer, what is the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD?$

![](images/bc/bc9f32a9c0e8b042498a72e808a29274bd505e786d8ec43d0e0bc9888fdf6e44.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is the sum of the areas of the triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle ADC$ (see the illustration below).

![](images/ac/acd2e923a65d0821cd59ed8b8274ceb5fc38def896467e37c8b1d454f958699e.png)

 First, we find the area for $\triangle ABC,$ and get
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABC} & =\frac{1}{2}(42)(35)\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘} \\  & =735\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘} \\  & ≈432.022\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

Now we find the area for $\triangle ADC,$ and get
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ADC} & =\frac{1}{2}(20)(18)\operatorname{sin}⁡{80}^{∘} \\  & =180\operatorname{sin}⁡{80}^{∘} \\  & ≈177.265\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

Finally, we add together the areas of our two triangles to determine the area of $ABCD.$ We get
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABCD} & ={A}_{ABC}+{A}_{ADC} \\  & =432.022+177.265 \\  & ≈609\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, to the nearest integer, the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is $609.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating the Area of a Quadrilateral

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
The area of $ABCD$ is $300\, \text{cm}^2.$  What is the area of $\triangle ABC$ rounded to the nearest integer?

![](images/c0/c06ffb123bdd24c3f83419767b6d1578223b8093089b79f91aae8f1fc6121305.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's start by finding the area of $\triangle ACD.$ We get 
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ACD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot DA\cdot DC\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡D \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(25)(32)\operatorname{sin}⁡{70}^{∘} \\  & =400\operatorname{sin}⁡{70}^{∘} \\  & =375.877... \\  & ≈376\,{\text{cm}}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

The difference of the areas of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ and $\triangle ACD$ gives the area of $\triangle ABC.$ Therefore, 
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABC} & ={A}_{ACD}-{A}_{ABCD} \\  & =376-300 \\  & =76\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Area of a Triangle Given the Area of a Quadrilateral

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Consider $\triangle ABC$ with sides of lengths $a,b,$ and $c,$ as shown below.

![](images/1d/1d30e12e2252b27a651bb02b718cf2214c7ddcf4f0e768c5bd952c11b2e4ecde.png)

Let's now add the height of length $h$ perpendicular to $\overline{BC},$ as shown.

![](images/96/96817ab2168b9ec37777166a26001ee8bc7e7709f80fdf234ac6d70cdfbb5ddc.png)

Using the usual formula for the area $\mathcal A$ of a triangle in terms of its base and height, we have

$$
\mathcal A = \dfrac12 ah.
$$

Using elementary trigonometry, we have that

$$
\dfrac{h}{b} = \sin C
$$

which means that 

$$
h = b\sin C.
$$

Therefore, by substituting this into our expression for $\mathcal A,$ we have

$$
\mathcal A = \dfrac12ab\sin C
$$

as required.

We can use a similar approach to prove the following formulas:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}bc\operatorname{sin}A \\ A & =\frac{1}{2}ac\operatorname{sin}B\end{aligned}
$$
